analysis.one_liner: Fully retrofits public housing to zero-carbon standards and lifts the ban on building new public housing.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 58 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was sent to the House Financial Services Committee and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would send federal grants to public housing agencies to deeply retrofit every public housing unit — insulation, heat pumps, all-electric appliances, solar panels, battery backup, and replacement of lead- and PFAS-contaminated water pipes — with a 10-year commitment to make the entire stock zero-carbon. It would require union-scale prevailing wages on all the work, reserve a rising share of jobs for public housing residents and contracts for resident-owned businesses, fund resident stipends, childcare, and services, and repeal the Faircloth Amendment, the 1998 rule that has barred construction of new public housing units. Funding was authorized at "such sums as necessary" to clear the public housing repair backlog, plus $1 billion for administration.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income public housing residents gain the most: healthier and safer homes, lower energy bills, on-site childcare and senior centers, free high-speed internet, a voice through elected resident councils, and first claim on the jobs the retrofits create. Construction workers gain through Davis-Bacon prevailing wages, apprenticeship pipelines, and rules favoring direct employment over temp staffing. U.S. manufacturers of heat pumps, solar equipment, and efficient appliances gain because the bill requires American-made materials.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public housing residents and retrofit workers

how_it_helps.text: Provides grants for deep energy retrofits of public housing: super-insulation, heat pumps, all-electric appliances, efficient plumbing and lighting, plus replacement of water pipes when lead exceeds 1 part per billion or PFAS chemicals exceed EPA thresholds.

Repeals the Faircloth Amendment (Section 9(g)(3) of the Housing Act of 1937), which since 1998 has prohibited federal support for new public housing units, reopening the door to building public housing where the market fails.

Ties all funded work to prevailing wages under the Davis-Bacon Act, requires project labor agreements on jobs of $25 million or more, reserves at least 20% of construction hours for registered apprentices, and bars replacement of striking or locked-out workers.

Creates a workforce pipeline for residents: $250-per-week training stipends, childcare, financial literacy courses, preference for partnerships with unions and apprenticeship programs, and reserved training slots for formerly incarcerated local residents.

Amends the Section 3 program so that at least 40% of jobs created rise to 90% must go to low- and very low-income people, and 20% rising to 50% of contract dollars must go to resident-owned businesses, with federal reporting to track it.

Protects residents from displacement: relocation assistance and a guaranteed right to return, a ban on any net loss of public housing units, and a requirement to finish replacement units before demolishing old ones.
Lets public housing agencies keep 90% of profits from selling renewable energy they generate, with residents of larger developments voting on how the money is used.

Adds community amenities to the eligible uses: childcare and senior centers, universal 100Mbps public internet, community gardens, electric vehicle charging, a bicycle for every low-income resident, and on-site clinics and affordable groceries.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through open-ended appropriations — the bill authorizes 'such sums as necessary' to clear the public housing capital backlog plus fiscal years 2024–2034 funding and $1 billion for administration, with no offsetting revenue. Gas utilities and makers of gas stoves and fossil-fueled heating equipment lose sales as units are electrified, and electric utilities lose some revenue as public housing generates its own renewable power.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; gas and utility sellers

drawbacks.text: The funding is open-ended: 'such sums as necessary' to cover the capital backlog, plus ten years of annual funding and $1 billion for administration, with no revenue source or spending cap, so the cost to taxpayers was unlimited on paper.

The requirements are rigid and stacked: by year three, 90% of generated jobs must go to low- and very low-income people and 50% of contract dollars to resident-owned businesses, and every applicant must commit to full decarbonization within 10 years — mandates that many under-resourced public housing agencies may struggle to meet, delaying projects.

The application process is heavy: two public comment periods (one lasting 90 days), four hearings, a community impact assessment, quarterly accounting to Congress, and signed approvals from both resident councils and local unions before an agency can even apply.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly one million households in U.S. public housing — largely low-income families, seniors, and people with disabilities — the bill offered a direct, material upgrade: safer homes, lower utility bills, and paid pathways into construction careers, funded at federal expense. The cost is real but diffuse (unlimited authorized appropriations spread across taxpayers), and the delivery risk is real: the bill piles mandates, quotas, and process requirements onto agencies that often lack staff, which could slow or botch the retrofits. Honest supporters would have to acknowledge that the open-ended funding and rigid quotas were the price of ambition, and the main reason the bill was never treated as viable.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing or vote until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced the bill on March 21, 2024, with 57 original cosponsors from her own party, eventually reaching 58 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, which holds jurisdiction over public housing.
The committee took no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Supporters of the status quo came out ahead: the federal government keeps spending nothing on the public housing repair backlog, no new public housing can be built under the Faircloth Amendment, and gas heating and utility sellers keep their existing market in public housing. Taxpayers avoided the bill's open-ended cost, but public housing residents got no relief from unsafe, unhealthy, energy-wasteful homes.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: no backlog spending, no new units

for.name: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 57 original cosponsors on introduction day.

for.name: 58 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Democrat and none came from the Republican majority.

against.name: Patrick McHenry
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the committee's action history ends with the referral.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor and committee agendas in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: No Republican member cosponsored the bill and the Republican-controlled committee process never advanced it, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 58 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled Financial Services Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have funneled grant-funded retrofit work to contractors under Davis-Bacon prevailing wages, apprenticeship quotas, and Buy American rules — profitable work, but with labor standards that direct the gains to workers. Its death means none of that work was commissioned.

industries.industry: Gas utilities and fossil-fuel heating equipment makers
industries.note: Electrification mandates would have replaced gas stoves, gas water heaters, and fossil-fueled HVAC in every public housing unit, permanently removing that equipment market. The status quo — in which these sales continue in aging public housing — is what prevailed.

Public housing would have generated its own solar power and kept 90% of the profits from selling surplus energy, cutting into utility sales. Utilities' existing role as the sole seller of energy to public housing was preserved by the bill's failure.

Agencies would have been the sole recipients of the grants, plus up to 5% of funds for their own capacity and a share of $1 billion for administration — locking in their role as the channel for federal housing money while imposing strict conditions on them.

industries.industry: Heat pump, solar, and battery manufacturers
industries.note: The bill required U.S.-made materials and mass procurement of heat pumps, efficient appliances, rooftop solar, and energy storage — a large guaranteed customer in public housing. It never passed, so no orders materialized.
